title: The lost Picou music
summary: They discuss where Picou's arrangements went, and Milton recalls how hard the advertising number was to play.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: We interviewed him about two years ago, and at that time he said he had several numbers arranged.
His wife died, I mean, you know, last week, two weeks ago.
I talked over his... I was talking about Piku. Which wife was that the died?
Ike Roberson's wife. Oh, Ike Roberson. Yeah, his wife had three weeks ago. Oh yes, I remember.
Well, I didn't know nothing until after the funeral was over. Nobody didn't tell me anything.

But I asked Piku's daughter about that music. I went there a couple weeks ago, and she said that she didn't think he had any of it. She'd never seen it. That Piku's first or second wife, I think he had about three wives before he died. I think his second wife had had it over on Leray Street when he lived there. Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. She'd never seen it after that.
And Twanette, Twanette, something like that.
Yeah, yeah. So I'm praying that music is all gone now.
He has some... He has some...
I'm telling you, he made for us many good records, numbers. I mean, he composed for us.
He talked about these four numbers. He had the Celestine's band to try to play it when they worked at the paddock. He said they couldn't play it at all.

That might be the number I'm talking about. Could be some of the same ones. Yeah, same number I'm talking about. I'm afraid they're lost. We stood on that number, I mean, very near a week. Because I had a certain beat I had to make, I mean, and the trambone player, the trambone player was the one he had the last part, you know what I mean? There's a little ending on it, like a coda or something on the other. Yeah. Yeah. And all that part, he had to make, that was something. I had to come in right with, I mean, I had to make them, if I would make them beat even with the trams, I mean, it wouldn't be there. I mean, I had to make them beat, I mean, even with that trams on. When we played it on that advertising, the fellas would get away from us when we played that, we didn't stay there. Was that out on the wagons on the street? Yeah, we used to play that on advertising. Yeah. Yeah, we'd have a special advertising number. A special advertising number. Howard tried to give it and everything, and people would never give it to nobody. Nobody would ever give it to anybody. That's too bad.
Nobody would ever give it to anybody.
